summary: Registers the application/dicom MIME sub-type for Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine data, such as medical images. The encoding itself is defined by the DICOM standards committee. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Doctors' scan files get a name tag so email and web programs know what they are.

questions: what is the dicom mime type
how to send medical images by email
subtitle: Registers the application/dicom media type for medical imaging data.

tldr.problem: Medical imaging systems create DICOM files, but email and web applications do not recognize them. Without a registered MIME type, these systems cannot reliably exchange images.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the application/dicom MIME media type with IANA and specifies its parameters, encoding, file extensions and magic numbers.
tldr.outcome: Email clients, web servers and other software can now properly identify, handle and transport medical images as application/dicom media.

today: RFC 3240 remains the official IANA registration for DICOM media type. The registration enables healthcare providers and vendors to reliably exchange medical images via email and web services worldwide.

sections.title: What is DICOM?
sections.content:
Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) is a standard for medical images, reports, and waveforms used in healthcare. Doctors use it to store X-rays, CT scans, MRIs and other medical data. A DICOM file contains image pixels, patient information, and technical details about how the image was taken.

Healthcare providers and vendors need to exchange DICOM files via email and web services. For this to work reliably, Internet applications must recognize the file format. That is what a MIME media type does: it labels what kind of data is in a message or file.
sections.plainLanguage: A doctor's scan is stored in a special format called DICOM. To email it, the email system needs to know 'this is a DICOM file' the same way it knows '.jpg' means a picture.

sections.title: The DICOM Media Type
sections.content:
This RFC registers application/dicom as the MIME media type for DICOM files. The type has one required parameter: id, a file identifier path. The id is taken from the DICOM File ID, limited to 71 characters total, with path components separated by forward slashes. For example: ROOTDIR/SUBDIR1/MRSCAN/A789FD07/19991024/ST00234/S00003/I00023.

Each path component uses only uppercase letters, digits and underscores, with a maximum of 8 characters per component. The special file DICOMDIR (which indexes other DICOM files) has an id of DICOMDIR. When a DICOMDIR is sent, other files it refers to must also be included.
sections.plainLanguage: The media type gets a label like 'application/jpeg' for pictures. DICOM's is 'application/dicom' and it has an address showing where the file is in a folder structure.

sections.title: Encoding and Transport
sections.content:
DICOM data is binary, so it must be encoded for email transport. The RFC recommends Base64 encoding, which converts binary to text characters safe for email. When multiple DICOM files are sent together, they use the Multipart/related container, or Multipart/mixed if mixed with other file types.

The RFC specifies magic numbers and file extensions: DICOM files start with a 128-byte preamble followed by the marker 'DICM' in ASCII. The recommended file extension is .dcm for regular files. Macintosh systems can use the file type code 'DICM'. These identifiers help systems recognize DICOM files even if metadata is missing.
sections.plainLanguage: The binary scan data gets dressed up in email-safe text (Base64). If you look at the first bytes of a real DICOM file, you'll see 'DICM' as a signature—like a watermark proving it's the real thing.

sections.title: Privacy and Security of Medical Data
sections.content:
DICOM files contain sensitive medical information: images of patients' bodies and demographic data. The RFC emphasizes that DICOM exchanges should be restricted to secure networks or wrapped in security protocols like S/MIME that protect patient confidentiality according to local laws and policies. The specific security mechanisms are the responsibility of the users, not the media type itself.

The RFC notes that generic email applications may not understand DICOM, so deployment in healthcare must ensure receiving systems have DICOM-aware software. However, the registration allows DICOM-aware and generic applications to interoperate: DICOM tools can read and interpret the data, while generic tools can at least save it in a recognizable form.
sections.plainLanguage: Medical scans are private. Hospitals must not send them over plain email like postcards. Doctors' programs know to keep them secret, but a regular email app might not, so be careful.

sections.title: Registration Details and Usage
sections.content:
The RFC is formally registered with IANA, the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, which maintains the official registry of MIME types. The registration lists the media type as 'Common' in intended usage, for the interchange of biomedical images between healthcare systems. It identifies the DICOM Standards Committee as the standards body and provides a contact person.

The registration enables web servers, email systems, and software to handle DICOM files appropriately: recognizing the type, applying correct content-transfer-encoding, routing to DICOM-aware applications, and preserving the file structure across networks. Implementation is not required for DICOM files to exist, but the registration provides standardized interoperability when systems exchange them.
sections.plainLanguage: The official registration makes it official: whenever a system sees 'application/dicom', it knows 'this is a medical scan' and can treat it right—keeping it private, letting the right programs read it, and not mangling it in transit.
